paras: The lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King took place early on June 10, 1882, at Lawrence, Kansas, when a masked mob broke into the Douglas County jail and hanged the three Black prisoners from the Kansas River bridge. The men were awaiting trial for the murder and robbery of David Bausman, an Ohio farmer. A coroner's inquest named four men as members of the mob, and Lawrence's Black residents held a mass meeting condemning both the murder and the lynching.

Bausman had come to Lawrence in late May to be near two brothers in Douglas County and was said to carry the money from the sale of a farm in Ohio. According to the accounts, he showed a roll of bills in a saloon, and King, a roustabout there, plotted with Vinegar and Robertson to rob him. Vinegar's daughter, called "Sis," was accused of luring him to an old icehouse by the river, where King and Robertson were said to have killed him with a hammer and club and thrown his body in the river.

After the body was found, Vinegar and his daughter were arrested, Robertson was caught at Independence, Missouri, and King was taken near Eudora. Even then a wire report said "a desperate attempt was made to lynch King," which the jailer frustrated. At a preliminary examination before Justice Neil on June 9 the accused were reported to have confessed, though one later account said only the woman, King and Robertson did.

About 1 a.m., by the Lawrence Journal's account, fifty or more armed men, most of them masked, came to the jail; other reports put the number at about a hundred. Sheriff Asher refused them entry, and the men cut through the doors and cell locks with sledge hammers and cold chisels. Deputy Sheriff Estes was halted at gunpoint, and a Journal reporter was sent to Estes's house for the keys, but the last lock had been cut before he returned.

The mob voted on whether to take Sis Vinegar as well and, after a tie, left her in the jail. The three men were marched about a square to the iron wagon bridge, Robertson falling to his knees to beg for mercy, and Vinegar protesting that he was innocent. From the middle of the bridge they were thrown over one by one; when King asked to be let down easy, the men behind him answered, "Did you let Bausman down easy?" Passengers getting off the midnight Santa Fe train were held until the hanging was over, and a crowd that could not get near cheered the lynchers as they returned.

Coroner Morris had the bodies cut down and carried to the jail yard, where hundreds of people came to see them. At his inquest David Kennedy, De Witt Ludington, Charley Apitz and Tob Miller were identified as associated with the mob, and a June 12 dispatch said the grand jury had indicted four of the mob. No report of an arrest or trial of any lyncher appears in the coverage.

Wire reports spoke of "talk of revenge on the part of the colored people" and of threats in North Lawrence against the mob's leaders. On the evening of June 12 a mass meeting of Black citizens condemned the murder, pointed to the help colored men had given in the capture, and resolved that the accused "were entitled to trial and sentences in due course of law." The meeting also urged Black residents to avoid expressions that might add to the excitement.

White papers across the country carried the story within days, mostly as wire copy that called the dead men "negro murderers" and treated their guilt as settled. A St. Louis dispatch headed "Merited Their Fate" said the lynching followed because the men's confessions had "conclusively shown" their guilt. The New Haven Morning Journal and Courier reported regret that the town had been "disgraced" but no sympathy for the prisoners, whom it called "cowardly, shrinking wretches."

In Kansas, the Emporia News first reprinted the Lawrence Journal's account, which ended by saying citizens were thankful that three "roughs" were gone. A week later its editorial called the lynching "a high-handed outrage," argued that the men were sure of conviction, and warned of retaliation by Black residents. Southern papers used the case against Kansas, with the Winston Western Sentinel remarking that a Southern state would have faced "howling" and the Russellville Democrat that "Kansas has begun to lynch her negro citizens." Several digests, from Wisconsin to Dakota Territory, also reported that the Black citizens' meeting had denounced the lynching.

One wire gave the hour as ten o'clock, but the local accounts place the jail break around midnight to 1 a.m. The Lawrence Journal said the lynchers were thought to come from the Bausman brothers' neighborhood with some Lawrence help, yet it also printed an assertion that two-thirds of the party were black men, while noting that a few were "simply blacked." Accounts also differ on whose neck was broken and when the bodies were cut down, at about 2 a.m. by the coroner or about 7 a.m.

reader.title: Lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King
bases: A masked mob broke into the Douglas County jail and hanged three Black prisoners accused of murder from the Kansas River bridge (A5, A8, A21, A27).

Fifty to more than a hundred masked men forced the jail over the sheriff's resistance and hanged three men awaiting trial for the murder of David Bausman, as punishment for that alleged crime (A8, A21, A27, A6).
The Lawrence Journal's local and eyewitness accounts (A21, A27), the AP-style wire (A4, A13) and separate long narratives (A5, A8) agree on the jail break and the triple hanging from the bridge.

accounts.gist: The reporter heard the sledges, was held inside the mob's guard line, fetched the keys from Deputy Estes's house, and saw the prisoners led to the bridge; afterward the crowd was allowed to look at the bodies.

accounts.gist: The lynching happened because the men's own confessions and the examination testimony had 'conclusively shown' them to be Bausman's murderers.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'Three Negro Murderers Hanged from a Bridge in View of a Train Full of People' treated the accused's guilt as settled.
The St. Louis dispatch ran under 'Merited Their Fate' and 'The Why of the Lynching'.
The New Haven account reported 'deep regret' that the town was 'disgraced' but 'not a word of sympathy' for the 'cowardly, shrinking wretches'.
The Emporia News's first report ended with Lawrence citizens 'thankful' that three 'roughs' were gone.
The Emporia News editorial called it 'a high-handed outrage' and mob rule 'a return to the ways of the lowest barbarism'.
Southern papers used it against Kansas and the North: 'If Kansas had been a Southern State there would have been howling'.
